Смотреть невозможно, это по сути своей индийское кино с белыми людьми. Вот мы стебем индусов за дурацкие боевики, где машины переворачивают, музыка постоянно вылезает, долгие переглядывания с намеком на гей порно, но в итоге смотрим тоже самое, но от итальянцев и говорим, что это классика. Ну это смотреть больно: драка одной рукой, отстреливание шляп и падение их с высоты как будто это самолёт, зажигалка в виде спины ковбоя, злодейский смех под детскую шкатулку. Ну это же олигофрения чистой воды, голый пистолет на фоне этого это «крестный отец». Это в прямом смысле перестроечное кино, что обозревает Антон VHS на ютубе. Посмотрите этот фильм, а потом тот же «воздушные пираты» 92го. Однозначно в истории кино накопилось много фильмов, и мы по прошествии лет можем и должны переосмыслить списки, что из года в год повторяют критики уже десятилетиями, и почему-то пафосно перефасовывают местами позиции. А может надо выкинуть половину? А «современную классику» на две трети? Поверьте есть много отличных фильмов, менее известных тех же лет, но до сих выглядящих актуально и увлекательно.

سکانس ابتدای فیلم که مرد ترسناک قصه وارد کافه میشه، از بارتندر میپرسه این آدمی که براش جایزه گذاشتن کجاست. بعد از تهدیدش، بارتندر میگه نمیدونم، ولی با دست به بالای سرش اشاره میکنه، یعنی طرف طبقه بالاست. اولا بارتندرهای کلاسیک خیلی مقتدرتر بودن و به این سادگی وا نمیدادن. خودشون بخش مهمی از قصه بودن. ثانیا، چرا اشاره میکنه؟جاسوسی وجود داره، یا نکنه اون مرد طبقه بالا صداشو میشنوه؟ در ادامه میبینیم که مرد ترسناک قصه، که هنوز اسمشم نمیدونیم، بدون هیچ پنهان‌کاری یا تلاش برای سر و صدا نکردن، از پله‌ها بالا میره. پس نیازی به پنهان کاری نبوده:) من معمولا مشکلات دوربین رو سخت متوجه میشم. ولی جایی که اولین قتل فیلم اتفاق میفته، مقتول قبلش آروم میخواد بره سمت چپ. حرکت میکنه. قاتل، تفنگ رو به سمت راست حرکت میده:))))))) یعنی بدیهیات کارگردانی رو بلد نیست. وسترن برای من ژانر مقدسیه. ده ها المان جذاب داره. از تفنگ و اسب بگیر تا کافه های خاص و عشق های جذابش. وسترن کلاسیک هیچوقت از جذابیت جسمی زن استفاده نکرد. ولی اولین بار تو این فیلم، دیدم که دقیقه ۱۰ نشده یه زن نیمه‌لخت تو فیلم داریم:) وقتی کمیت کارگردان لنگ باشه، این چیزا طبیعیه. متنی که تا اینجا نوشتم بعد از دیدن کمتر از ۱۱ دقیقه از فیلم نوشتم و این همه ایراد داشت. بعد میگن چرا با دیدن ۱۰ دقیقه از فیلم، میگی فیلم بده! ژانر وسترن، منطق اکشن داره. یعنی انگیزه‌هایی وجود داره که باعث میشه آدم‌ها دست به قتل بزنن، یا نزنن. مثلا اگر طرف حساب تو، کلانتر شهر باشه، سعی میکنی تا جای ممکن نکشیش چون خلاف قانونه و دردسر داره برات. ولی با قرار گرفتن در موقعیت بهتر، تهدیدش میکنی که به خواسته‌ت برسی. در ریو براوو، این منطق اکشن در تک‌تک لحظه‌ها هست‌. وقتی جان وین رو نمیکشن و مجبورش میکنن بره سمت کلانتری، بخاطر آزاد کردن رفیقشونه. وگرنه میکشتنش. این مقدمه رو گفتم برای سکانس بعدی فیلم. سکانس اولی که کلینت ایستوود رو میبینیم، چند نکته مضحک وجود داره. اولا به راحتی آدم مورد نظرش رو شروع میکنه به کتک زدن، و هیچ کدوم از آدم‌های دیگه دخالت نمیکنن. آدم‌هایی که در سایر فیلم‌های وسترن، حداقل نصفشون نقشی فراتر از سیاهی لشکر یا مترسک داشتن و موضعشون مشخص بود. اما اینجا فقط نظاره‌گر ان. ۳ تا از دوستای اون آدمی که ۲۰۰۰ دلار براش جایزه گذاشتن، میان دم در و اسلحه به دست، ایستوود رو تهدید میکنن. ایستوود پشت به اونهاست. هیچ دلیلی وجود نداره که نکشنش. هیچ دلیلی نداره که بهش بگن ولش کن بره. میتونن راحت بکشنش. ولی صبر میکنن، و قهرمان قصه ما هم برمیگرده و هر ۳ تا رو میکشه تا به جایزه‌ش برسه! وسترن‌های کلاسیک به ظاهر خیلی ساده‌ن، ولی وسترن اسپاگتی بهمون ثابت میکنه که این سادگی در واقع پر از پیچیدگیه و ساختنش کار هرکسی نیست. فیلم در ادامه بدتر و بدتر شد و دیگه حوصله نوشتن راجع بهشو نداشتم.

Lighting and lens are very sharp. Sets and locations are great too. The dusty towns and wide open environments really help sell the western atmosphere. The sound design also feels old school. It lacks bass, I think. Everything sounds high pitched. Dialogues are obviously dubbed or rerecorded in the studio because some lines do not sync with the movements of their lips. The musical score sounds heroic, but emotionally I did not really feel it connecting with the story. Even by the end, I never fully felt the tension or triumph that the film was aiming for.

"Alive or dead? It's your choice..." And it's also your choice whether or not to believe that this film it's good because it's of my opinion that this film is meh. However, it is leagues better than it's successor even though it gets a similar star rating. What I like about this film, like its successor, is the aesthetic of the film. The old wild west motif, the wild west set designs, and the wardrobe of that time are just a chef's kiss. However, what also needs to happen beyond that is there needs to be good/interesting and exciting characters as well as a good story that moves well. Unfortunately that isn't necessarily the case with this film like its successor. Although the Clint Eastwood and Lee Van Cleef characters are entertaining, sort of makes you appreciate them in following film more, the other characters in the film are boring and add virtually nothing to the overall story. They were all pretty boring besides the little boy at the hotel helping Eastwood's character as well as the old man living by the train tracks. Something I really find annoying in these films is the stupid hat shooting bit they do. It's obviously edited and fake thus making it super annoying and boring. Next segment already please! I also thought that this film was WAYYYYY TOO long and SLOOOW. There was no need for either of them regardless of the type of story they were trying to tell versus what they were actually telling. I didn't care that much for the film based on what I saw early on and so I didn't really pay attention for most of it. I honestly don't see the hype of these films one bit. They're not entertaining enough for me, they're too slow, too long, and not a whole lot in the character department in my opinion. All in all I also think that Sergio Leone is an overrated director just like Kubrick.

Ok 90% of that movie makes way more sense when you realize that even though it’s the SAME ACTOR playing the villain as in a fistful of dollars, he is NOT Ramon, he is in fact Indio. I now feel silly for grunting slyly at the TV “aim for the heart, Ramon”. The excessive macho dick measuring contests for a little stale by the end. It felt like every scene was a standoff or sharpshooting some obscure object without flinching. It lost its gravitas. There were also way too many schemes to coherently follow. Even insignificant side characters had an agenda to throw the train of thought off the tracks. It was a knot of plot twists that you couldn’t untangle. Also, why’d the bitch shoot herself when she could’ve just as easily shot el Indio. Seemed unwarranted and could’ve given el Indio a more powerful backstory if there was a more relatable backstory, or at least fed into the psycho side more. He’s literally crying over some girl he raped after sliming her man. Showing any emotion at all feels contradictory to his character, but perhaps this adds to the chaotic nature of his character. Also, I know this was the 60s, but the Rojos and El Indio is just mental. Red and Indian? Like Indians are the cliche villain in Westerns, but to call Mexicans Indians in their own language seems like a unnecessary shot fired. Regardless of the over saturation of the macho, the colonel was a sweet addition. Threatening the macho of our Manco was refreshing. The cinematography felt like it took more of an advantage of the landscape, and the opening and closing shots were some of my favorites (for of a person shot off a horse in the opening, colonel riding off into the sun at end). The opening credits also had an intriguing graphic that flowed along the landscape. Fun. Color on set, lighting, and costuming felt a little more bland than fistful, but the night effects were better with the blue light as opposed to just darkening the screen in fistful. This feels like a movie that’s far more interested in looking cool than actually being engaging. I can appreciate the style and the atmosphere it’s going for, but after a while it just becomes exhausting watching grown men constantly stare each other down in silence trying to radiate aura. There are so many scenes built around forced macho energy, leaning against walls with cigarettes, slowly provoking each other while trying to light a smoke, dragging out every interaction like it’s supposed to feel legendary. It’s not cringe exactly, but it becomes obnoxious because the movie keeps repeating that same energy over and over without giving much else underneath it. The acting is decent enough for what the film is trying to do, but the characters themselves barely left an impression on me. They feel more like archetypes posing for cool shots rather than fully interesting people. Dialogue is minimal and often exists more to maintain the “cool factor” than to actually build depth or tension. Visually, I’ll give the movie credit. The production design is easily its strongest aspect. The dusty towns, costumes, interiors, and overall western atmosphere are well done and help sell the world. You can see the influence this style of western had on cinema afterward. But outside of the presentation, I found the actual experience pretty underwhelming. The pacing drags badly, scenes stretch on far longer than they need to, and the entertainment value just isn’t there for me. It constantly feels like the movie is waiting for you to admire how cool everything looks rather than pulling you into the story itself. And honestly, without heavily borrowing from older Japanese cinema, I’m not sure the film really has enough substance to stand strongly on its own. Beneath all the style and attitude, there just isn’t much that genuinely grabbed me. **The 10-Point Evaluation** Acting: 6 Dialogue: 5 Story: 5 Complexity: 4 Impact & Inspiration: 2 Characters: 3 Music: 2 Production Design: 8 Entertainment: 3 Pacing: 3 Cinematography: 3 4/10 There’s undeniable style and atmosphere here, but the film spends so much time trying to look cool that it forgets to be consistently entertaining.

For a few dollars more had potential to be more interesting than a fistful of dollars, but something about the execution left me wanting for more. For starters, the soundtrack for the most part exceeds the original. The gimmick with the pocketwatch helped to build anticipation during the duels  and also gave the scenes a little more emotional weight to them. In contrast to the usual epic western music, the quiet tune puts us in the shoes of the characters a little. The additional layer of melancholy in the music allows us to reflect on the brutality of these duels, and to see them for what they really are: People killing each other. I also think it was a brilliant idea to introduce another lone cowboy into the mix. Lee Van Cleef is just as effortlessly cool as Clint Eastwood and I was excited to see what kind of rivalry will spawn when two capable bounty hunters set their sights on the same target. We get a little bit of that when they first meet but they pretty much get along for the rest of the film. I just feel like that limited the opportunities for creative interactions they could've had, and took away alot of the intrigue I had from the start of the film. Another thing is I'm just not sure I like the story beats here as much as I like the ones in fistful of dollars. This is just a little messy compared to the straightforward traditional hero's journey in the first one. I also think both the Colonel and Indio's backstories and motivations could've been a little better fleshed out. There are definitely ways of doing that without nessecarily stripping away the mystery of the two characters. This would've made the final duel feel a bit more impactful and given it the sauce it needs to surpass the third act of the first film. I think the thing with Leone is that he has such a brilliant style but sometimes he just gets a little too carried away with it. Enough that there's an abundance of style but not enough substance. I still like these westerns but the problem is I can't love it as much as I want to. Maybe I'll change my mind with the good, the bad and the ugly

Two bounty hunters walk into the desert, discover they have the same hobby, and decide the logical solution is to compete over who can kill more people. For a Few Dollars More is basically cowboy LinkedIn, except the networking events involve revolvers and the job offers come with corpses. Clint Eastwood’s Man with No Name barely speaks, barely reacts, and somehow manages to have more charisma than everyone in the film combined. Meanwhile, Lee Van Cleef’s Colonel Mortimer arrives looking like he has been personally designed by God to wear a black hat. And then there’s the pocket watch. A tiny musical pocket watch somehow becomes one of the most sinister objects in the entire movie. Every time that melody starts playing, you know somebody’s about to have a really bad afternoon. The best part is the chemistry between Eastwood and Van Cleef. They’re not exactly friends. They’re more like two extremely competent coworkers who have accidentally been assigned the same murder project. And Sergio Leone knows how to stretch a moment until you’re practically holding your breath. The close-ups, the silence, the music, the ridiculous amount of dust — everything feels bigger than life.

One thing that never disappoints is Morricone’s score. He carries. Yeah, Leone is capturing the story and everything else really great but the story itself is pretty bland. Bland and drab. Perhaps it’s because I’ve seen many of his films by now (so I know what he is capable of) but they all are the same. (He doesn't go to any new length here.) -> As much as you can call it coherence you can argue for repetitiveness. And I don’t think he is proving (most of all for himself) for either a cause or a point in this one. It is pretty standardised at this point and therefore loses a bit of necessary touch - not to mention magic. What should be seen as grand is closer to being the opposite. Not only does it HAVE but it furthermore FOLLOWS a rather grounded notion while approaching it as something far differently. Differently as in spirituality. The thing is though, I don't see either Leone or the film ever meeting those demands. Everything falls flat while suggesting something else. . . At this point, it has an expectancy over it. As in, you can (kind of) expect where it’s going. Hence it’s quite difficult for Leone to surprise you. Especially given how firm he is in keeping the same old formula when it comes to his pictures. It’s quite redundant… He’s able to keep me on the edge only for his superb camera work and how the lot is (more or less) staged. Staged before the camera that is. But that will only take him so far. And given how much the picture depends on a well structured narrative, I fail to see the - or any - brilliance. Not when I keep on asking the film about what either drives or simply motivates the other. Is it the characters and the events that they meet or could it be how the film is able to encapsulate it? Again, I fail to see both the relevance and, arguably more importantly, the result. When I watch a film I would like to know why they are describing it. When it comes to “A few Dollars More” I am lost. The idea of avarice comes into mind but whether greed is a blessing or a curse, that I don’t know. Nor does the film. Perhaps that uncertainty, vagueness really, is not only the point but driving force to it. Nonetheless such grey-zone upsets me. Why? Simply because the characters are anything but secure in both their position and following mindset. Their confidence seems to overrule any bit of shady footing from the filmmakers and where the film wishes to make a point. And why I esteem Leone as one of the best. Or rather when I think he is at his best. It would be when he includes the emotional value and emotional scope. Preferably at the same time. In “A few Dollars More”, it’s low on any emotion. Especially one directed at the audience. Instead, it looks like Leone aims for more flashy and epic moments. Epic moments, might I add, lead to complete nothing of value for me given the lack of both build up and emotional attachment. - - It’s like the product ought to be harsh in its outline. And that is one saving grace to why I don’t think it’s a dud. Still, I don’t fancy it even though it’s masterfully made (in some details). There is a false sense of tension here. A tension that not betrays but fundamentally lacks emotion. And comparing the suspense we’re getting here with Leone’s other pictures, if not movies in general, this is quite low. Not only is it the suspense but the film itself isn’t that special. If anything, this film is relatively corked. Especially when comparing it to Leone’s other film as well as given where this film aimed towards. The lack of women is so acute that it becomes a thing itself. So much so that in the end, these dudes fight over the lady. Their lost romance. I would’ve liked if they, in other words Leone, had dived deeper into that. Into the romantic sort of affair and not have the looting be the main source of interest.

Après avoir vu Pour une poignée de dollars que je n'avais pas trop adoré, lui préférant d'ailleurs largement Yojimbo de Kurosawa, je viens de finir Et pour quelques dollars de plus, le deuxième de la trilogie, avant d'aller découvrir Le Bon, la Brute et le Truand au cinéma en 4K ce soir. Contrairement au premier volet un peu plus artisanal, ce film est beaucoup plus froid, méthodique et perfectionné. L'histoire suit deux chasseurs de primes rivaux aux méthodes opposées qui se retrouvent sur la même piste : celle de l'Indien, chef de gang psychopathe évadé qui prépare le braquage de la banque d'El Paso. D'un côté, on a Monco (Clint Eastwood) qui chasse pour l'appât du gain pur et dur, et de l'autre le colonel Douglas Mortimer (Lee Van Cleef), guidé par une vengeance personnelle et intime. Le cœur du film repose sur cette cupidité. Sergio Leone oppose le matérialisme décomplexé de l'Amérique naissante avec Clint qui compte chaque cadavre en dollars au code d'honneur chevaleresque et tragique de Mortimer, pour qui l'argent ne vaut rien face au sang versé. Côté acting, c'est du lourd. Clint Eastwood affine son mythe en pure économie de mouvements, mâchoire serrée sur son cigare, regard plissé sous le chapeau : du vrai aura farming qui fait le contrepoids parfait au reste du casting. Lee Van Cleef a un profil d'aigle, un port altier et un regard d'acier teinté de mélancolie et d'aristocratie, avec une autorité naturelle qui lui permet presque de voler la vedette. Gian Maria Volontè livre une performance fiévreuse, constamment sous l'emprise de la fumette avec ses rires sardoniques et ses folies meurtrières. Mention spéciale à la surprise de voir Klaus Kinski dans le rôle du bossu Wild ! Visuellement, Leone maîtrise ses très grands angles panoramiques dans le désert d'Almería, avec des coupes brutales vers des gros plans assez extrêmes sur les yeux, les fronts moites et les mains gantées. La musique d'Ennio Morricone vit à l'intérieur de l'histoire, complètement diégétique via la boîte à musique de la montre à gousset, véritable symbole du temps, de la mémoire et du trauma : quand la mélodie s'arrête, on sait que ça sent mauvais. Le climax final est un pur opéra, la caméra tournant autour des tireurs en suivant les montées chromatiques des trompettes et des cloches. Un très bon film, j'espère que Le Bon, la Brute et le Truand sera à la hauteur de celui-là.

Even though it is widely considered and quite rightly so that The Good, the Bad and the Ugly is the best of the Dollars trilogy. For me my favourite of this trio hands down is this absolute masterpiece of cinema. Lee Van Cleef, Clint Eastwood, and Gian Maria Volonté exude extreme cool from the opening scenes to the climatic end duel, all of them bringing commanding performances. So many iconic shots, sequences, and lines of dialogue have fully imprinted themselves into my mind. Sergio Leoni was truly the master adapting Japanese cinema and here it's no less obvious in it brilliance and simplicity. The old school sound effects and Ennio Morricones iconic score permeating throughout is such a joy to the ears. I will never grow tired of watching this film, to me this is the iconic Western upon which all others must stand against.

Wow. I already thought the first one was great, but this is one hell of a step up. Genuinely a complete movie and one of the best westerns I've ever seen. The main reason being: it finally gets a notable side character, a memorable villain, and more complex / variable intentions among all parties. And the 'notable side character' arguably has just as much, if not more screen presence than Clint eastwood, which I never would've expected. Van cleef is fucking incredible in this movie and I couldn't believe someone could be more imposing than clint, in what is pretty much his film. Insane addition to the movie and changes everything about it. The contrast in their personalities and different approaches to the same problem that their characters make is so nice to watch, their dynamic is at its best with the hat shootout. And then you have indio and his gang, a memorable villain with a more nuanced backstory and intentions that always keep changing. It's a much better, more refined story that is less predictable yet easier to follow, and that's exactly what the first one was missing. The intro credits as usual are innovative and so cool. The cinematography is incredible, beautiful landscapes, stunning shot framing, insanely operatic showdowns and innovative camerawork. And the night sequences are especially stunning, I really mean it. Then you have the shootouts. It takes the showdowns of fistful of dollars to another level - longer, higher stakes, less predictable, and the score behind all of it elevates it to another level. One of the best western scores ever, and it is so essential to the movie here, it's incredible. I love how every character has his own sound motif, and the cherry ontop is the music box motif used so perfectly in the finale. The final showdown was just insane. As a whole, it's a complete movie that I can't fault in any way. It's decisively better than 'For a fistful of dollars', as good as it was. And after seeing 'The good, the bad and the ugly', I can confidently say that this one is the best of the 3. It's just got the formula totally nailed down, I see it as the perfect balance between the first and third movies - introducing the all-important van cleef, having a more nuanced story & memorable villain, yet retaining a more concise runtime, and not having to split the screentime across 3 main leads (I didn't like Wallach in TGTBTU that much). It's an amazing movie.

For a Few Dollars More de Sergio Leone est un chef d’œuvre. Ce western met en scène deux chasseurs de prime amenés à se rencontrer et à partager la même mission. Ainsi, Manco et le colonel Mortimer mettrons en place plusieurs stratagèmes pour mettre la main sur El Indio, venant de s’évader de prison, ainsi que sa bande. Cette seconde réalisation pour la trilogie du Dollars est à mon sens la meilleure. On nous donne deux acteurs d’exemptions ( Clint Eastwood et Lee Van Cleef ) amenés a travailler ensemble contre El Indio ( joué par Gian María Volonté ). L’intrigue est très bonne et met en place un scénario super bien fondé. Ici, il sera beaucoup plus question de justice mais avec quelques contraste, Manco fait justice et s’enrichit tandis que Mortimer est à la recherche d’une réel justice. La Vengeance est ici le thème principal du film et il sera amenés au fur et à mesure avec des flashbacks. La mélodie de la montre est aussi un son iconique du film ainsi qu’un élément centrale du film. Beaucoup de scènes sont iconique et représentent énormément de chose, comme la scènes des chapeau qui n’est pas une scène de duels mais plutôt de démonstration pour savoir qui est le meilleur. Le film nous montre que la vengeance peut rapidement devenir une prison, Mortimer se venge mais le passé ne change pas, il n’obtiendra donc qu’une victoire amère.
